c.tagline: Wales's compact capital of castles, choirs, and rugby roar.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed Hackney (black/blue) cabs are metered and can be hailed or picked up at ranks; private-hire cars such as Dragon Taxis and app rides (Uber, Bolt) must be pre-booked.

emergency.note: 112 works throughout the UK and Europe and connects to police, fire, and ambulance; 999 is the traditional UK emergency number.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The St Mary Street nightlife strip gets rowdy with drunken crowds late on weekends and rugby match days.

hood_desc: The walkable heart around Cardiff Castle, the Principality Stadium, the covered Victorian arcades and St David's shopping centre; best for first-timers who want everything on the doorstep.
Cardiff Bay (Butetown): a redeveloped waterfront around Mermaid Quay and the Wales Millennium Centre, with restaurants, bars, and boat trips; good for waterside dining and evenings out.
A leafy, village-like district of Victorian terraces, independent cafes, delis, and Pontcanna Fields; suits travellers wanting a relaxed, foodie, local base a short walk from the centre.
The student quarter beside Cardiff University and the Civic Centre's museums; lively, budget-friendly, and very central.
A residential area around Roath Park and its boating lake, with the Wellfield Road cafes and independent shops; calm and family-friendly.
lodging: voco St. David's Cardiff by IHG

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality.

transit.hours: Cardiff Bus services run from roughly 5:00 AM to around 11:00 PM, with some late-night routes on weekends; Transport for Wales trains run from early morning to late evening.
transit.note: Cardiff Bus is the main city operator, with Transport for Wales running local rail (the Valley Lines network) from Cardiff Central and Queen Street stations. The compact centre and Cardiff Bay are easily walked or reached by a short bus or train hop.
transit.pay: Pay the bus driver by contactless card or cash, or use the Cardiff Bus app; trains are paid by ticket, contactless, or the TfW app. Multi-operator day tickets allow unlimited travel across city bus routes.

car.idp: Not required for short visits (EU/US licences accepted)

train: Cardiff Central & Cardiff Queen Street (Transport for Wales and GWR; direct trains to London Paddington and the Valley Lines local network)

landmarks: Cardiff Castle
Two thousand years of history stack a Roman fort, Norman keep, and flamboyant Victorian-Gothic fantasy apartments by William Burges in the very heart of the city.
Cardiff Bay
Europe's largest waterfront regeneration transformed the old Tiger Bay docks into a buzzing freshwater bay of promenades, restaurants, and landmark modern architecture.
Wales Millennium Centre
The bronze-armored 'Armadillo' opera house crowned with giant bilingual poetry inscriptions stages world-class performances and symbolizes modern Welsh cultural confidence.
Principality Stadium
Rugby's most atmospheric cathedral, its retractable roof rising over the River Taff downtown, shakes with 74,000 voices singing on Six Nations match days.
National Museum Cardiff
A grand neoclassical museum pairing Wales's natural history with one of Europe's finest Impressionist collections, including Monets and Renoirs, all free to visit.
St Fagans National Museum of History
Over forty rescued historic buildings, from Celtic roundhouses to a miners' institute, re-erected across parkland make this beloved open-air museum Wales in miniature.
Bute Park
A 130-acre green ribbon of arboretum lawns and riverside paths behind the castle, once the Marquess of Bute's private grounds, now Cardiff's leafy playground.
Llandaff Cathedral
Tucked in a hollow by the Taff, this medieval cathedral blends Norman arches with Jacob Epstein's striking aluminum Christ soaring above the nave.
Victorian and Edwardian Arcades
Seven glass-roofed shopping arcades, the oldest from 1858, lace the city center with independent boutiques, record shops, and the legendary Spillers Records.
Senedd and the Norwegian Church
On Cardiff Bay's waterfront, the Welsh Parliament's glass-and-slate Senedd stands near the white timber church where author Roald Dahl was christened.

train.note: No international trains - Eurostar runs from London St Pancras. GWR reaches London Paddington in about 1h50 from Cardiff Central, and Transport for Wales runs the Valley Lines commuter network plus the slow but scenic route north to Shrewsbury and Holyhead. Cardiff Queen Street handles most local services. Advance fares open 12 weeks out.

bus.note: No direct international coaches. National Express (https://www.nationalexpress.com/) and Megabus (https://uk.megabus.com/) run from Cardiff Central bus interchange beside the station to London in about 3h30, Bristol in an hour and Swansea in 1h15. For Ireland, coaches connect to the Holyhead or Fishguard ferries.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Cardiff - the old Swansea-Cork route closed years ago and Cardiff docks handle cargo. The Cardiff Bay waterbus to Penarth and Mermaid Quay is a short local hop. For Ireland, sail from Fishguard or Pembroke Dock in west Wales, both reachable by train.

half.name: Brecon Beacons National Park
half.blurb: Mountain range of grassy peaks, waterfalls and reservoirs in south Wales, a popular hiking and stargazing destination.

half.name: Big Pit National Coal Museum
half.blurb: Former working coal mine in Blaenavon where retired miners lead visitors 300 feet underground on guided tours.

half.name: Caerphilly Castle
half.blurb: Wales's largest castle, a moated 13th-century fortress with concentric walls and a leaning tower rivaling Pisa's.

half.name: Tintern Abbey
half.blurb: Ruined 12th-century Cistercian abbey in the Wye Valley whose roofless nave inspired Wordsworth's poetry and Turner's paintings.
